title_en: Beijing Xiyou Lighting Equipment Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Municipal Commerce Committee — dispute over administrative decision
ruling_gist_en: The greatest characteristic of e-government that distinguishes it from traditional administrative methods lies in the paperless nature of administrative procedures and the networking of information transmission. Where a party, after accepting an administrative processing method in the form of e-government, subsequently claims that the administrative agency's failure to serve a written decision on it constitutes a procedural violation, the People's Court shall not support such a claim.

full_text_en:
Beijing Xiyou Lighting Equipment Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Municipal Commission of Commerce — administrative decision dispute

【Ruling Summary】

The greatest characteristic of e-government, as distinct from traditional administrative methods, lies in paperless administrative procedures and the networking of information transmission. Where a party, after accepting an administrative processing method that is electronic and government-based, subsequently claims that the administrative procedure was unlawful on the ground that the administrative authority did not serve a written decision upon it, the people's court shall not support such a claim.

Plaintiff: Beijing Xiyou Lighting Equipment Co., Ltd., domiciled at Huixinli, Chaoyang District, Beijing.
Legal Representative: Jiang Ruiguo, Chairman of the Board.

Defendant: Shanghai Municipal Commission of Commerce, domiciled at Loushanguan Road, Changning District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Sha Hailin, Director of the Commission.

Third Party: Shanghai Pudong International Airport Import & Export Co., Ltd., domiciled at Wei 1st Road, Pudong Airport, Pudong New District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Hu Jianming, Chairman of the Board.

Third Party: Shanghai Airport (Group) Co., Ltd., domiciled at Qihang Road, Pudong Airport, Pudong New District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Wu Nianzu, Chairman of the Board.

Third Party: Shanghai ABX Lighting Equipment Co., Ltd., domiciled at Longwu Road, Minhang District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Geoffrey Hall, Chairman of the Board.

The plaintiff, Beijing Xiyou Lighting Equipment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xiyou Company), dissatisfied with the administrative decision of the defendant, the Shanghai Municipal Commission of Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the Municipal Commerce Commission), as published in the winning bid announcement No. 0681-0840ZBJ08022 dated December 29, 2008, initiated an administrative lawsuit with the Changning District People's Court of Shanghai.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The plaintiff was a bidder in the international tendering project for high-mast lighting poles for the apron of the west terminal, maintenance apron, and cargo apron of the Shanghai Hongqiao International Airport expansion project. The evaluation method for the project was the lowest evaluated bid price method. The plaintiff submitted the lowest quotation among all bidders but was evaluated as a technical disqualification. Pursuant to the provisions of the Ministry of Commerce Order No. 13, the "Measures for the Implementation of International Tendering for Mechanical and Electrical Products" (hereinafter referred to as "Order No. 13"), the plaintiff submitted written objections to the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, on multiple occasions. The defendant made a decision instructing the tendering agency to conduct a re-evaluation. The newly selected experts again evaluated the plaintiff's bid as a technical disqualification, but changed the reasons. The defendant's subordinate Mechanical and Electrical Products Import Office approved this and published the winning bid announcement on December 29, 2008. The plaintiff contended that after receiving the plaintiff's objection, the defendant only made an announcement online but did not respond to the plaintiff's objection, which was procedurally unlawful. The reason relied upon by the new bid evaluation committee in concluding that the plaintiff's bid remained a technical disqualification was that the illumination uniformity ratio in certain areas of the illumination calculation report in the bid documents did not meet the requirements of the tender documents and the mandatory civil aviation industry standards. This reason changed the disqualification reason from the first evaluation, violating Article 41(3) of Order No. 13, which provides: "The public announcement of the bid evaluation result is a one-time public announcement; any unsuccessful bid reasons not publicly announced shall no longer serve as the basis for disqualification or unsuccessful bid." The defendant failed to fulfill its supervisory and review duties during the process of handling the objection. The number of experts on the re-evaluation committee did not reach five as required by Order No. 13. Moreover, among the re-evaluation committee members, there was a representative of the tendering agency, a certain Ju Mou, who had also participated in the first evaluation, thereby compromising the fairness of the re-evaluation. The tender documents did not explicitly specify the requirement for "illumination uniformity ratio in other areas of the apron," yet the disqualification reasons in both evaluations cited this requirement, which was improper. In summary, the defendant failed to exercise lawful and effective review and supervision over the re-evaluation reasons and the experts on the bid evaluation committee, resulting in unfairness in the re-evaluation. The plaintiff requested the revocation of the specific administrative act of the winning bid announcement No. 0681-0840ZBJ08022 issued by the defendant on December 29, 2008.

Defendant's Defense: The defendant is the competent authority in Shanghai for international bidding of mechanical and electrical products. It manages and provides services for international bidding of mechanical and electrical products through the bidding network in accordance with the "Tendering and Bidding Law of the People's Republic of China," Order No. 13, the "Provisions on Further Regulating International Bidding Activities for Mechanical and Electrical Products," and other relevant legal provisions. The defendant lawfully accepted the objection submitted by the plaintiff, Xiyou Company, through the bidding network and made a decision to instruct the tendering agency to organize a re-evaluation. After the experts re-evaluated and still determined the plaintiff's bid as disqualified, the defendant, upon review, concluded that the re-evaluation procedure fully complied with Order No. 13. The defendant operated on the bidding network, made a decision to uphold the original bid evaluation result, and the network automatically generated the objection handling result immediately, notifying the plaintiff in the form of a "High-mast Lighting Pole Winning Bid Announcement." The defendant argued that both Order No. 13 and the bidding documents in this case explicitly stipulate that international bidding for mechanical and electrical products shall complete the relevant bidding procedures, including expert selection, public announcement of evaluation results, and objection handling, on the bidding network. The defendant, in accordance with these provisions and the online operation procedures designed by the Ministry of Commerce, lawfully accepted the plaintiff's objection and made a handling decision in the form of an online announcement, thereby performing its duties lawfully and with full procedural legality. The reasons for disqualification in the re-evaluation were consistent in content with those in the first evaluation, differing only in expression; therefore, they cannot be considered beyond the scope of the original disqualification reasons. Moreover, the experts participating in the re-evaluation had the independent authority to reach their own evaluation conclusions without being bound by the first evaluation's conclusions and reasons. The provisions of Article 41(3) of Order No. 13 do not apply to re-evaluation. Laws and regulations do not vest the defendant with the authority to conduct substantive review of the opinions of the expert panel in the re-evaluation committee; the defendant only supervises and coordinates the bidding evaluation procedure. Upon review, the experts were selected online randomly again. Among them, four were national-level experts, and the other, Ju Mou, was a representative of the tenderee and the tendering agency. The composition of the re-evaluation committee fully complied with Order No. 13. During the objection handling process, the defendant had reviewed the tender documents as required and found no circumstances affecting the fairness of the evaluation results, hence it made the decision to uphold the original evaluation result. In summary, the specific administrative act of the defendant was based on clear facts, correctly applied the law, and was procedurally lawful. The defendant requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

The third party, Shanghai Pudong International Airport Import & Export Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Pudong Airport Company), stated agreement with the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, and argued that Article 41(3) of Order No. 13, which states "the public announcement of the bid evaluation result is a one-time public announcement; any unsuccessful bid reasons not publicly announced shall no longer serve as the basis for disqualification or unsuccessful bid," applies only to the first evaluation process. The evaluation result made by the newly formed expert review committee is not subject to this provision, i.e., it is not bound by the first disqualification reasons. The selection of evaluation experts was done through online operation, and the Ministry of Commerce has enforced the random selection function through the bidding network electronic platform. The tendering agency and the owner cannot arbitrarily designate experts beyond the constraints of the bidding network platform. Both the "Tendering and Bidding Law of the People's Republic of China" and Order No. 13 clearly stipulate that the bid evaluation committee shall consist of experts, representatives of the tenderee, and representatives of the tendering agency, forming a single number of five or more persons. The identity of Ju Mou in both the original and the re-evaluation committees was that of a representative of the tenderee and the tendering agency, which fully complies with the regulations. Clause 2.1.13.9 of the tender documents did not explicitly set a requirement for the illumination uniformity ratio in other areas of the apron, but the "Technical Standards for Civil Airport Movement Areas" in the tender documents did have such a requirement, and this standard is a mandatory civil aviation industry standard. After re-evaluation, the plaintiff's bid documents did not meet this mandatory civil aviation industry standard. In summary, the third party requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

The third party, Shanghai Airport (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Airport Group Company), stated agreement with the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, and the third party, Pudong Airport Company, and requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

The third party, Shanghai ABX Lighting Equipment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as ABX Company), stated agreement with the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, and the third party, Pudong Airport Company. The plaintiff argued that the defendant's specific administrative act was unlawful but could not provide legal basis to prove it, and requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

Facts Found by the Court of First Instance, Changning District People's Court of Shanghai:

The third party, Airport Group Company, entrusted the third party, Pudong Airport Company, to procure high-mast lighting poles for the expansion project of an international airport through international tendering. The tendering project was opened on September 8, 2008, with three enterprises participating: ABX Company, E Lamp Factory, and the plaintiff, Xiyou Company. After evaluation by the bid evaluation committee organized by the tendering agency, ABX Company was recommended as the winning bidder. The evaluation result was publicly announced on the bidding network on October 7, 2008. The evaluation conclusion for the plaintiff was: technical disqualification. The reason was: the illumination uniformity ratio in areas such as the road surface between the apron and the terminal building was greater than 4:1, not meeting the requirement of Clause 2.1.13.9 of Chapter 8 of the tender documents. The plaintiff, dissatisfied with the evaluation result, argued that the tender documents did not contain any requirement for the illumination uniformity ratio in areas such as the road surface between the apron and the terminal building, and therefore the disqualification reason was unfounded. Accordingly, on October 13 and October 28, 2008, the plaintiff submitted written objections to the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, twice, requesting a re-evaluation. On December 10, 2008, the defendant made an objection handling decision on the bidding network, ordering a re-evaluation, requiring the tendering agency to strictly organize experts for re-evaluation in accordance with the regulations. In accordance with the defendant's requirement, the tendering agency organized a new bid evaluation committee to conduct a re-evaluation. The conclusion of the new bid evaluation committee was still a technical disqualification, with the reason being that the illumination uniformity ratio in certain areas of the illumination calculation report in the bid documents did not meet the requirements of the tender documents and the mandatory civil aviation industry standards. After receiving the re-evaluation expert report submitted by the tendering agency, the defendant made a decision to "approve the experts' re-evaluation opinion and uphold the original evaluation result" and filed the re-evaluation report online on December 29, 2008. The bidding network immediately generated a winning bid announcement for high-mast lighting poles, which stated: "After re-evaluation, ABX Company is the final winning bidder for the international tendering project for high-mast lighting poles for the apron of the west terminal, maintenance apron, and cargo apron of an international airport expansion project." On December 31, 2008, the defendant issued the "Notice of International Bid Evaluation Result" through the bidding network. Based on this notice, the tendering agency issued a notice of award to the winning bidder and notified other bidders of the result, while also returning the bid bonds to all unsuccessful bidders. Dissatisfied, the plaintiff initiated the administrative lawsuit in question.

The above facts are confirmed by evidence submitted by both the plaintiff and the defendant.

Issue in Dispute at First Instance:

Whether the decision made by the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, to uphold the re-evaluation result was lawful.

Opinion of the Court of First Instance, Changning District People's Court of Shanghai:

Pursuant to the "Tendering and Bidding Law of the People's Republic of China," Order No. 13, the "Provisions on Further Regulating International Bidding Activities for Mechanical and Electrical Products," and other relevant legal provisions, the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, as the competent administrative authority for international bidding activities for mechanical and electrical products, has the statutory authority to accept objections and make administrative decisions.

This case is a new type of case arising from e-government. The dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant over whether the specific administrative act complied with statutory procedures is essentially a disagreement between traditional and modern modes of government administration. In today's rapidly developing information technology society, the emergence of e-government is a result of information technology influencing government administrative methods. E-government can be understood as a new mode of modern government administration. This method, through the application of information technology, is conducive to improving public services, enhancing public participation, government transparency, and democratic levels, promoting office automation, electronification, networking, and comprehensive sharing of information resources, and improving the efficiency of public management and the scientific nature of public decision-making. The greatest characteristic of e-government, as distinct from traditional administrative methods, lies in paperless administrative procedures, networking of information transmission, and virtualization of administrative legal relations. In this case, Article 6 of Order No. 13 explicitly provides that international bidding for mechanical and electrical products shall complete relevant bidding procedures, including expert selection, public announcement of evaluation results, and objection handling, on the bidding network. Moreover, the "International Competitive Bidding Documents for Procurement of Mechanical and Electrical Products" involved in this case also explicitly stipulate that international bidding for mechanical and electrical products shall conduct bidding procedures such as project filing, bid announcement publication, public announcement of evaluation results, and objection handling on the bidding network, and that bidders must successfully register on the bidding network before the bid deadline. Therefore, the plaintiff, Xiyou Company, was fully aware that international bidding for mechanical and electrical products and objection handling would adopt a networked approach. The plaintiff's decision to participate in the bidding project in question indicates its acceptance of the networked tendering and bidding method and the electronic government administrative handling method for relevant objection handling. The vehicle for an administrative decision can take various forms, either electronic or in writing. After an administrative authority makes an administrative decision, it may convert it into a paper document with text through computers or other automated devices and serve it on the administrative counterparty, or it may notify the counterparty through the network in the form of an electronic administrative decision. The counterparty may also print the administrative decision on paper using a printer. However, the original purpose of e-government is to improve administrative efficiency and save administrative costs. If all administrative acts were to require paper documents as a formal requirement, the advantages of computer technology in improving administrative efficiency could not be realized. Of course, the form of an administrative act made by an automated device should also comply with the general requirements of procedural law regarding form. After reviewing the re-evaluation, the defendant, the Municipal Commerce Commission, made an administrative decision in the form of an announcement on the network, which complied with the procedural provisions of Order No. 13. Order No. 13 does not provide that when an administrative decision is made through the network, a separate written decision must be served on the counterparty. The plaintiff's claim, after accepting the electronic government administrative handling method, that the defendant's procedure was unlawful on the ground that the defendant did not serve a written decision upon it, lacks legal basis and is not accepted.

To determine whether the defendant's decision to uphold the re-evaluation result was lawful, the following issues must also be analyzed: first, review of the reasons for re-evaluation; second, review of the selection of experts for re-evaluation; third, review of the tender documents.

Regarding the review of the reasons for re-evaluation. Article 41 of Order No. 13 provides: "After the bid evaluation is completed, the tendering agency shall publish the bid evaluation result on the bidding network for a period of seven days. The tendering agency shall fill in the 'Public Announcement Table of Bid Evaluation Results' with the unsuccessful bid reasons for each bidder in terms of commercial, technical, and price evaluation. The content filled in must clearly specify the requirements of the tender documents and the bidder's response. The 'Public Announcement Table of Bid Evaluation Results' includes items such as 'Recommended Winning Bidder and Manufacturer Name,' 'Evaluated Bid Price,' and 'Unsuccessful Bid Reasons,' and shall be consistent with the bid evaluation report. The public announcement of the bid evaluation result is a one-time public announcement; any unsuccessful bid reasons not publicly announced shall no longer serve as the basis for disqualification or unsuccessful bid, except for technical deviations of bidders who did not participate in technical evaluation due to commercial disqualification." This article mainly sets forth normative requirements regarding the time and content of the first public announcement of bid evaluation results, rather than requirements for re-evaluation. The legislative intent of Article 41(3) of Order No. 13 is to restrict the conduct of the first bid evaluation committee, requiring that once a decision is made, it cannot be changed arbitrarily, and that unsuccessful bid reasons must be publicly announced, thereby binding the evaluation committee to carefully handle the evaluation process. From the textual structure of Order No. 13, Articles 41 to 51 are procedural rules organized chronologically. Article 50(2) of Order No. 13 provides: "Once the competent authority's handling opinion on the objection is made, it shall take effect immediately and a public announcement of the result shall be made." If a bidder still has objections, it can only seek remedy through reconsideration or litigation, and cannot cyclically apply Articles 41 to 50. Therefore, a tendering project can undergo re-evaluation at most once. The provision in Article 41(3) that "the public announcement of the bid evaluation result is a one-time public announcement; any unsuccessful bid reasons not publicly announced shall no longer serve as the basis for disqualification or unsuccessful bid" clearly applies only to the first evaluation and does not apply to re-evaluation. The purpose of establishing the re-evaluation procedure is to conduct a completely fresh evaluation unaffected by the first evaluation. For a completely independent newly formed review committee, it would be manifestly unreasonable for its evaluation result to be constrained by the previous evaluation result, and would also be contrary to the legislative purpose of Order No. 13. The plaintiff's claim that the re-evaluation violated Article 41(3) of Order No. 13 and therefore requested the revocation of the specific administrative act of the defendant cannot be sustained.

Regarding the review of the selection of experts for re-evaluation. Article 33(1) of Order No. 13 provides: "The bid evaluation committee shall consist of experts in technical, economic, and related fields with senior professional titles or equivalent professional level, and representatives of the tenderee and the tendering agency, forming a single number of five or more persons, of which the number of experts in technical, economic, and other fields shall not be less than two-thirds of the total members." Article 49(2) provides: "Experts for re-evaluation shall be randomly re-selected from the national-level expert pool. If national-level experts are insufficient, they may be supplemented from the local-level expert pool, but the number of national-level experts shall not be less than two-thirds. The number of experts participating in the re-evaluation shall not be less than the number of experts who participated in the previous evaluation. The re-evaluation result shall be filed with the corresponding competent authority." According to the evidence submitted by the defendant, the re-evaluation committee in this case consisted of five members, including four experts and one representative of the tenderee and the tendering agency. The four experts were all national-level experts, meeting the requirement of at least two-thirds of the total members, and their number was not less than the four experts who participated in the first evaluation. The bid evaluation committee as provided in Order No. 13 consists of experts and representatives of the tenderee and the tendering agency, forming a single number of five or more persons. It is not, as the plaintiff contends, a committee composed of five experts only. Representatives of the tenderee and the tendering agency are also members of the bid evaluation committee. Article 34 of the Ministry of Commerce's "Provisions on Further Regulating International Bidding Activities for Mechanical and Electrical Products" provides: "Experts for re-evaluation shall not include experts who participated in the previous evaluation or reviewed the tender documents." This provision is targeted at experts only and does not impose requirements on representatives of the tenderee or the tendering agency on the bid evaluation committee. The identity of Ju Mou in both the first evaluation committee and the re-evaluation committee was that of a representative of the tenderee and the tendering agency. The laws and regulations mentioned above do not provide that a representative of the tenderee or the tendering agency who participated in the first evaluation is prohibited from participating in the re-evaluation. The plaintiff's argument that the participation of a representative of the tenderee and the tendering agency who participated in the first evaluation in the re-evaluation compromised fairness lacks legal basis.

Regarding the Review of Bidding Documents. Article 33 of the *Further Regulations on Standardizing International Bidding Activities for Mechanical and Electrical Products* issued by the Ministry of Commerce clearly stipulates: "If, during the handling of a challenge, it is found that important commercial or technical clauses (parameters) in the bidding documents contain errors, are contradictory, or inconsistent with relevant national laws and regulations, thereby affecting the fairness of the bid evaluation results, the current tender shall be deemed invalid, and the competent authority shall publish this on the bidding website." Although Article 33 of Decree No. 13 provides that bid evaluation is the responsibility of the bid evaluation committee, the defendant, the Municipal Commission of Commerce, as the competent authority, has the obligation to review the bidding documents. In the bidding documents involved in this case, there was no explicit requirement for the "illuminance uniformity ratio for other areas of the apron", but the bidding documents clearly stipulated that "the design, manufacturing, inspection, testing, and acceptance standards for all provided equipment shall comply with the standards already implemented by the International Organization for Standardization and relevant domestic and international industries." Among these, the *Technical Standards for Aerodrome Areas of Civil Airports* was one of the standards referenced in the bidding documents. This standard was issued by the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC), and the CAAC's *Notice on Promulgating the Technical Standards for Aerodrome Areas of Civil Airports*, effective June 1, 2006, explicitly stated that the standard is a "mandatory civil aviation industry standard", i.e., a standard that must be complied with. Although the bidding documents did not explicitly require the "illuminance uniformity ratio for other areas of the apron", given that the *Technical Standards for Aerodrome Areas of Civil Airports* has clear requirements for the illuminance uniformity ratio, there is no contradiction between the two. Therefore, the bidding documents did not exhibit "errors in important commercial or technical clauses (parameters), contradictions, or inconsistency with relevant national laws and regulations." The claims of the plaintiff, Xiyou Company, cannot be sustained.

In summary, the specific administrative act of the defendant, the Municipal Commission of Commerce, in upholding the original bid evaluation results was based on clear facts, conclusive evidence, lawful administrative procedures, and correct application of law. The plaintiff, Xiyou Company's, claim that the challenged specific administrative act was unlawful and its request for its annulment are not supported by sufficient factual evidence or legal basis and are therefore not granted. Accordingly, the Changning District People's Court of Shanghai, pursuant to Article 56, Paragraph (4) of the Supreme People's Court's *Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, rendered the following judgment on January 15, 2010:

The claims of the plaintiff, Xiyou Company, are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 50 shall be borne by the plaintiff, Xiyou Company.

Xiyou Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, insisting on its original trial claims and requesting the annulment of the appellee, the Municipal Commission of Commerce's, decision to uphold the original bid evaluation results after reviewing the re-evaluation opinion. Its main grounds for appeal were: The factual basis for the bid rejection was insufficient; after the re-evaluation, changing the reason for bid rejection from the failure to meet the asterisked terms in the bidding documents during the initial evaluation to other reasons not specified in the bidding documents was baseless; the reason for bid rejection was invalid. The re-evaluation was a procedural step in handling a challenge to the initial evaluation within a single bidding process and should be governed by Article 41, Paragraph 3 of Decree No. 13, and other provisions. Since the original reason for bid rejection was found to be invalid after the re-evaluation, this indicated that the appellant's challenge had merit, and the bid should not have been rejected based on a new reason. The appellee failed to provide evidence of supervision over the selection process of experts for the re-evaluation. Furthermore, the re-evaluation should have been based on the opinions of an expert panel rather than constituting a new bid evaluation committee; the participation of an individual surnamed Ju as an expert in the re-evaluation violated regulations. According to Decree No. 13, if a bidder objects to the evaluation results, it must submit a written document in addition to raising a challenge online. Therefore, this case did not purely concern e-government. After receiving the appellant's challenge, the appellee failed to serve the appellant with a decision regarding the challenge, nor did it inform the appellant whether the challenge was accepted or whether a re-evaluation was initiated, thus its administrative procedure was unlawful. The appellant requested the court of second instance to overturn the original judgment and grant its original trial claims.

The appellee, the Municipal Commission of Commerce, argued: It adhered to its defense at first instance. The appellee's review and decision regarding the re-evaluation were based on clear facts, correct application of law, and were within its statutory authority and procedure. It requested the court of second instance to uphold the original judgment.

The third party at first instance, Pudong Airport Company, stated: It agreed with the opinion of the appellee, the Municipal Commission of Commerce. An airport must pass a professional acceptance inspection by the CAAC before official operation. The technical specifications of the products provided by the appellant, Xiyou Company, failed to meet the mandatory requirements of the CAAC. It requested the court of second instance to uphold the original judgment.

The other third parties at first instance, Airport Group Company and Abikesi Company, both stated their agreement with the opinion of the appellee, the Municipal Commission of Commerce, and requested the court of second instance to uphold the original judgment.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, upon trial at second instance, confirmed the facts found at first instance.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held at second instance:

Pursuant to the *Tendering and Bidding Law of the People's Republic of China*, Decree No. 13, the *Further Regulations on Standardizing International Bidding Activities for Mechanical and Electrical Products*, and other provisions, the appellee, the Municipal Commission of Commerce, had the statutory authority to supervise international bidding activities for mechanical and electrical products within its jurisdiction and to render the administrative decision in question. Based on the facts of this case, after accepting the challenge from the appellant, Xiyou Company, the appellee instructed the bidding agency to conduct a re-evaluation. During the review of the re-evaluation report, the appellee, in accordance with the law, supervised and reviewed the contents of the bidding documents, the composition of the re-evaluation expert panel, and the re-evaluation opinion. It determined that the re-evaluation report complied with legal requirements and rendered a decision agreeing with the re-evaluation opinion and upholding the original bid evaluation results. This administrative act was lawful. The appellee published the decision on handling the challenge via the re-evaluation on the bidding website, legally reviewed the re-evaluation report before making its decision, filed the re-evaluation report online, and generated the relevant high-mast lighting tender award announcement. The administrative procedure was also proper.

Based on the information in the materials concerning the experts for the re-evaluation in this case, including their names, positions, level in the expert database, and number, the composition of the expert panel for the re-evaluation met legal requirements. The appellee, the Municipal Commission of Commerce's, defense argument that the design procedures of the online system were sufficient to ensure the randomness and fairness of expert selection should be accepted. The appellant, Xiyou Company's, ground of appeal that the appellee should have conducted on-site supervision over the expert selection process for the re-evaluation lacks legal basis. Its challenges regarding the agency responsible for the re-evaluation and the composition of the bid evaluation committee also lack sufficient factual and legal basis and cannot be sustained.

The opinion of the court of first instance that Article 41, Paragraph 3 of Decree No. 13 applies only to the initial bid evaluation and not to a re-evaluation was correct. The appellant, Xiyou Company's, ground of appeal that changing the reason for bid rejection during the re-evaluation violated Article 41, Paragraph 3 of Decree No. 13 cannot be sustained.

Relevant laws have clearly stipulated that the relevant procedures for bidding activities are to be completed on the bidding website. The appellee, the Municipal Commission of Commerce, has lawfully published on the bidding website the decision to handle the challenge by organizing an expert re-evaluation. After the re-evaluation, it filed the re-evaluation report online and generated the tender award announcement identifying the final winning bidder. By viewing the above information published on the bidding website, the appellant, Xiyou Company, would have been aware that the appellee had decided to uphold the original bid evaluation results after the re-evaluation. Therefore, the appellant's ground of appeal that the appellee should have directly served it with the decision regarding the challenge, as well as its challenges concerning related procedural steps, lack corresponding legal basis and are not adopted.

In conclusion, the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 61, Paragraph (1) of the *Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, rendered the following judgment on May 19, 2010:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

The appellate case acceptance fee of RMB 50 shall be borne by the appellant, Xiyou Company.

This judgment is final.
